pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Fossilised Dinosaur Dung / Coprolites (ages 7–9): a coprolite is fossilised dung (droppings turned to rock), and palaeontologists cut them open to find plant fragments, seeds, bones, or fish scales inside — direct evidence of what a dinosaur actually ATE.
• Standards — UK (DfE): 'working scientifically' (gather and interpret evidence to answer a question); builds on the trace-fossil category and herbivore/carnivore classification.
• Standards — US (NGSS): grade-3 3-LS4-1 (fossils as evidence of organisms and their behaviour — here, diet).
• Operational details — Coprolites are TRACE fossils (record of an activity: eating/digesting). The teaching value is that they give DIRECT dietary evidence, complementing the INDIRECT clue of tooth shape: teeth suggest what an animal COULD eat; coprolite contents show what it DID eat. Contents reveal diet — seeds and plant cell walls → herbivore; crushed bone → a bone-crunching carnivore (famously a T. rex coprolite full of bone); fish scales → a fish-eater. Address the 'ick' factor by framing it as prized evidence. Note the challenge: it's often hard to be sure WHICH dinosaur produced a given coprolite.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7): says a coprolite is fossilised dung and it tells us what a dinosaur ate. Tier B (~8): links contents (seeds vs bone) to plant- vs meat-eater. Tier C (~9): explains coprolites give direct diet evidence (vs teeth as indirect) and notes it's often uncertain which animal produced one.
bestPractices: Frame coprolites as prized DIRECT evidence of diet to convert the 'ick' reaction into scientific curiosity.
Contrast direct (coprolite contents = what it DID eat) with indirect (tooth shape = what it COULD eat) evidence — a clean lesson in evidence strength.
Have children read contents to a conclusion (seeds→plants; bone→meat; scales→fish), practising inference.
Flag the identification problem — you often can't be certain which species left a coprolite — to model honest uncertainty.
Use the memorable real case (a large bone-filled Cretaceous coprolite attributed to a T. rex) to make it concrete.
keyRepresentations: A 'slice and examine' view: a coprolite cross-section with visible seeds, bone bits, or scales under a lens.
A contents → diet inference card (seeds→herbivore, bone→carnivore, scales→fish-eater).
Side-by-side 'teeth clue (could eat)' vs 'coprolite clue (did eat)'.
A magnifier tool revealing microscopic plant/bone fragments.
commonMisconceptions: 'A coprolite is a body fossil / a stomach' — it's fossilised dung, a trace fossil recording feeding.
'Coprolites are worthless/just gross' — they are direct, high-value evidence of diet.
'Teeth already tell us exactly what it ate' — teeth show capability; coprolites show actual meals.
'We always know which dinosaur made a coprolite' — attribution is often uncertain.
'All dung fossils look the same inside' — contents differ (plants, bone, scales) and that's the whole point.

learn.summary: Children (ages 7–9) learn that a coprolite is fossilised dung — a trace fossil that records an animal's feeding — and that cutting one open can reveal contents (seeds and plant fibres, crushed bone, or fish scales) that give DIRECT evidence of what the animal that produced it actually ate, at least in that meal (mostly the tougher, less-digested parts survive). The central idea is contrasting this with the INDIRECT clue of tooth shape: teeth suggest what an animal COULD eat, while coprolite contents show what it DID eat. Learners practise reading contents to a diet conclusion (seeds→plant-eater, bone→meat-eater, scales→fish-eater), and also meet the honest limit that it is often uncertain WHICH animal produced a given coprolite.

activities.title: Slice and examine: read the coprolite's contents
feedback: If a learner reads seeds/plant fibres: confirm this points to a plant-eater (herbivore) — those are undigested parts of plants it swallowed.
If a learner reads crushed bone or scales: confirm this points to a meat- or fish-eater — those are the remains of prey, NOT pieces of the dinosaur's own skeleton.
If a learner thinks the bones are the dinosaur's own body: clarify that dung contains what was eaten and passed through; the bones belonged to the prey.
If a learner says dung cannot become a fossil: explain dung can be mineralised and preserved like other trace fossils, and the hardened contents are exactly what makes it useful evidence.
activities.rationale: The objective is an investigation — open, examine, deduce — so an examine-and-infer task where the learner selects evidence and states a conclusion is intended to build the reasoning rather than just name it. Dragging finds into an analysis panel and showing the reasoning is an optional way to make the inference visible. This is a proposed, untested design.
learnerActions: Receive a lumpy grey 'coprolite' specimen and the explanation that it is fossilised dinosaur dung turned to rock.
Open the specimen and sweep a magnifier across the cut face to find embedded contents — seeds and shredded plant fibres in one specimen, splinters of crushed bone in another, fish scales in a third.

Collect each find (optionally by dragging items into an analysis panel) and state the diet verdict it supports: seeds/plant fibres → plant-eater; crushed bone → bone-crunching meat-eater; fish scales → fish-eater.
Write or say the reasoning: 'the contents are the remains of what the animal ate, so this dinosaur was a ___.'
activities.intendedInsight: The things preserved inside fossilised dung are the remains of an animal's meals, so reading those contents lets you infer what the dinosaur actually ate.

activities.title: Teeth clue vs dung clue: could eat vs did eat
feedback: If a learner says teeth already tell us exactly what it ate: point out teeth show capability; the coprolite shows the actual meal, which can confirm or refine the tooth clue.
If a learner treats both as equally direct: note that one shows a preserved meal (direct) while the other is inferred from body shape (indirect).
activities.rationale: Contrasting a preserved meal (which the source identifies as direct dietary evidence) with a structural clue gives children a concrete, age-appropriate lesson in evidence type and strength. A paired comparison panel contrasting the two clues is an optional presentation that keeps the comparison explicit.
sourceClaims: Coprolites (fossilised dung) are trace fossils whose contents — plant fragments/seeds, bone, or fish scales — provide direct evidence of diet; a large bone-rich Cretaceous coprolite has been attributed to Tyrannosaurus rex. Attribution to a specific producer is often uncertain.
learnerActions: Look at an animal's teeth beside the contents of a coprolite thought to come from that kind of animal, presented side by side.
Say what the teeth suggest the animal COULD eat (capability) and what the coprolite shows it ACTUALLY ate (its real meals).
Explain in their own words why the coprolite is direct evidence of diet while the teeth are an indirect clue.
activities.intendedInsight: Tooth shape suggests what an animal was capable of eating, but coprolite contents are direct evidence of what it really ate — a comparison of indirect versus direct evidence.

activities.title: Whose dung was it? Modelling honest uncertainty
feedback: If a learner insists we always know which dinosaur made a coprolite: explain that attribution to a specific producer is often uncertain, even when the diet is clear.
Praise a learner who distinguishes the confident claim (diet) from the uncertain one (producer) — that is how real scientists report findings.
activities.rationale: Deliberately leaving attribution ambiguous models honest uncertainty and separates a well-supported inference (diet) from an under-determined one (species), a core 'working scientifically' habit. The source directly notes that attribution to a specific producer is often uncertain.
sourceClaims: Coprolites (fossilised dung) are trace fossils whose contents — plant fragments/seeds, bone, or fish scales — provide direct evidence of diet; a large bone-rich Cretaceous coprolite has been attributed to Tyrannosaurus rex. Attribution to a specific producer is often uncertain.
learnerActions: Examine a coprolite with clear contents (e.g. the famous large bone-filled Cretaceous specimen attributed to T. rex) and confidently state the DIET it shows.
Then try to name exactly which animal produced it, and notice how hard that is.
Say out loud what we can be sure of (the diet) and what remains uncertain (the exact producer), and why 'we're not sure' is a valid scientific answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Even strong evidence leaves some questions open: coprolite contents can firmly reveal diet while the exact animal that produced the dung often stays uncertain.

activities.title: Check: match contents to diet and explain the evidence
feedback: Correct answer for bone/scales: a meat- or fish-eater — the bones and scales are remains of its food preserved in its fossilised droppings; the contents are direct evidence of diet.
Correct answer for leaves/seeds: a plant-eater (herbivore).
If a learner cannot reason from contents to diet or thinks the contents are the animal's own body, return to the slice-and-examine activity before re-checking.
activities.rationale: Matching and short-answer items check the inference. They confirm whether a learner can classify contents→diet but do not by themselves elicit the learner constructing and justifying the inference, so they are intended to be used after the hands-on examination rather than instead of it.
learnerActions: Match coprolite contents to the diet they imply: seeds/plant fibres → plant-eater; crushed bone → meat-eater; fish scales → fish-eater.
Answer: 'What does crushed bone inside a coprolite tell us about the dinosaur that made it?' and explain how you know.
Transfer the reasoning to a new case: a coprolite full of chewed leaves and seeds — what kind of dinosaur made it?
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to map contents onto a diet, and explain why, confirms the inference transfers to new specimens.

activities.title: Optional: palaeontologist hands over a specimen
feedback: Prompt deeper if the learner states a diet without naming the evidence: 'Which contents led you to that?'
If the learner is over-confident about the producer, ask what else could have made dung with those contents.
activities.rationale: A Socratic exchange fits the inference and gives practice in justifying and qualifying a claim. It is offered as an alternative with a different purpose (verbal reasoning and confidence) and is intended to complement, not replace, the hands-on examination where the inference is intended to be constructed.
learnerActions: Take a coprolite from an expert who asks, 'What did this animal eat, and how sure are you?'
Describe the contents you can see and reason aloud toward a diet.
Respond to follow-up prompts about how confident you are and whether you can tell which animal made it.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating the inference and your confidence to a questioner strengthens the reasoning and the habit of qualifying claims.

constraints: Matching/recognition tasks can check that a learner classifies contents→diet, but recognition alone does not elicit the learner producing and justifying an inference; they are best used after the hands-on examination.
Attribution of a coprolite to a specific species is often uncertain; do not ask learners to name the exact producer as if determinable — ask what diet the contents show and what remains uncertain.
The slice-and-examine specimens model ideal evidence; frame the 'ick' factor as prized evidence and handle sensitively for this age group.
The hands-on examination design and any efficacy/sequencing wording are proposed, not empirically tested.
reviewNotes: This guidance was rewritten by an agent from the original row without fresh source verification; the single source is marked verified:false, so the T. rex attribution and contents-as-diet claims remain unverified here.
All activities are proposed/unvalidated designs; efficacy is stated with intended/may/proposed wording and should not be read as tested.

sourceClaims are retained only where the available (unverified) source directly supports the teaching point (the direct-evidence and attribution-uncertainty claims); activities whose rationale concerns only interaction or assessment format carry [] because the source does not establish format efficacy.

probeDeeper: If a coprolite was full of chewed-up leaves and seeds instead, what kind of dinosaur made it?
Why is fossilised dung sometimes better evidence of diet than the shape of an animal's teeth?
How could scientists be fairly sure the coprolite came from a dinosaur and not some other animal?
assess.correctAnswer: It was a meat-eater — it ate animals and fish. The crushed bones and scales inside are the remains of its food, preserved in its fossilised droppings (a coprolite). The contents are direct evidence of what the dinosaur ate.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dung is too soft or gross to fossilise: 'poo can't turn into a fossil, so this isn't real evidence.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that dung can be mineralised and preserved like other trace fossils; the hardened contents are exactly what makes it useful.
errorPatterns.distractor: Dung can't become a fossil, so this can't tell us anything real.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies a coprolite is a genuine fossil, or refuses to draw any conclusion from it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the contents as the animal's own body: 'the bones inside are pieces of the dinosaur's own skeleton.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify that dung contains the remains of what was eaten and passed through — the bones belonged to the prey, not the dinosaur.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bones inside are pieces of the dinosaur's own skeleton.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Attributes the bones and scales to the coprolite-maker rather than to its food.

errorPatterns.pattern: Denies diet can be read from droppings: 'you can't tell what an animal ate from its poo.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Walk through the inference: seeds mean plants eaten, bones mean animals eaten — the contents ARE the diet.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: States that dung reveals nothing about diet even when contents are described.

responseLevels.gap: Denies dung can fossilise, or says a coprolite reveals nothing about the animal.
responseLevels.full: Reads the contents as ingested food to infer diet (bones/scales mean carnivore) AND transfers the reasoning to the leaves-and-seeds case for a herbivore.
responseLevels.partial: Knows a coprolite is fossilised dung but cannot reason from its contents to the diet, or thinks the contents are the animal's own body.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Scientists cut open a fossilised lump of dinosaur dung and find crushed bones and fish scales inside. What can they tell about the dinosaur that made it, and how do they know?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands says the stuff inside is what the animal ate, so it was a carnivore. A child who doesn't thinks dung cannot become a fossil at all, or reads the bones inside as the dinosaur's own skeleton.
